1.q: וַֽ⁠יְהִי֙ בִּ⁠שְׁתֵּ֣י עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה בִּ⁠שְׁנֵי עָשָׂ֥ר חֹ֖דֶשׁ בְּ⁠אֶחָ֣ד לַ⁠חֹ֑דֶשׁ
1.note: Ezekiel is using the words translated as **And it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

1.q: בִּ⁠שְׁתֵּ֣י עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה בִּ⁠שְׁנֵי עָשָׂ֥ר חֹ֖דֶשׁ בְּ⁠אֶחָ֣ד לַ⁠חֹ֑דֶשׁ
1.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **twelfth** or **first**, you could represent these numbers in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in year 12, in month 12, on day 1 of the month]

The implication is that this was the twelfth year after King Jehoiachin and Ezekiel had been taken into exile in Babylon. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the twelfth year after King Jehoiachin and I had been taken into exile in Babylon]

The **twelfth** month of the Hebrew calendar includes parts of February and March on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew day and month into an approximate date on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the date will be different every year, and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the number of the day and the name of the month on the Hebrew calendar and say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar.
See how you translated this expression in 20:2.

2.note: See how you translated **Son of man** in [2:1](ta:02).

Yahweh is using **take up a lamentation over Pharaoh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “sing a funeral song about Pharaoh.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [sing a mourning song for Pharaoh]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a young lion** is strong and attacks other animals, so Pharaoh was powerful and attacked other nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [You were considered to be powerful and prone to to attack the nations, just as a young lion is strong and attacks other animals]

The expression **You were likened** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who did the action, it may have been other people or Pharaoh himself who made this comparison. Alternate translation: [People compared you to a young lion of the nations]

2.q: וְ⁠אַתָּה֙ כַּ⁠תַּנִּ֣ים בַּ⁠יַּמִּ֔ים וַ⁠תָּ֣גַח בְּ⁠נַהֲרוֹתֶ֗י⁠ךָ וַ⁠תִּדְלַח־מַ֨יִם֙ בְּ⁠רַגְלֶ֔י⁠ךָ וַ⁠תִּרְפֹּ֖ס נַהֲרוֹתָֽ⁠ם
2.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the sea monster** **stirred up the waters** with its **feet** and **muddied their rivers**, so Pharaoh used his power to cause trouble in Egypt and among the nations around it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [but you are like the sea monster in the seas, for just as it thrashes about in the water, so you use your power to cause trouble in Egypt and among the nations]

A **sea monster** is a kind of large, dangerous animal that lives in the water. If your readers would not be familiar with what a sea monster is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [are like a large creature that lives in the ocean]

3.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:4.

3.q: וּ⁠פָרַשְׂתִּ֤י עָלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ אֶת רִשְׁתִּ֔⁠י בִּ⁠קְהַ֖ל עַמִּ֣ים רַבִּ֑ים וְ⁠הֶעֱל֖וּ⁠ךָ בְּ⁠חֶרְמִֽ⁠י
3.note: Yahweh is speaking as if Pharaoh were a sea creature that he would catch in a **net** and pull out of the water in a **dragnet**. It means that Yahweh will use the armies of many peoples to capture and defeat Pharaoh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will capture you by means of an assembly of many peoples, and they will defeat you as I direct them]

4.note: Yahweh is using **on the face of the field** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the open field.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the open countryside]

4.q: וְ⁠הִשְׁכַּנְתִּ֤י עָלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ כָּל ע֣וֹף הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֔יִם וְ⁠הִשְׂבַּעְתִּ֥י מִמְּ⁠ךָ֖ חַיַּ֥ת כָּל הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
4.note: The implication is that the dead body of Pharaoh, pictured as a sea monster, would lie unburied, and birds and wild animals would eat it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And I will make every bird of the heavens dwell on your unburied dead body to eat it, and I will make the living thing of all the land satisfied from eating your flesh]

5.q: וְ⁠נָתַתִּ֥י אֶת בְּשָׂרְ⁠ךָ֖ עַל הֶֽ⁠הָרִ֑ים וּ⁠מִלֵּאתִ֥י הַ⁠גֵּאָי֖וֹת רָמוּתֶֽ⁠ךָ
5.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [And I will scatter the pieces of your dead body all over the mountains and valleys]

Yahweh says **I will fill the valleys with your carcass** as an extreme statement to emphasize how great the destruction of Pharaoh and his army will be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and I will scatter the dead bodies of your army in great numbers throughout the valleys]

6.note: Yahweh is speaking of **the land of your outflow** as if it were a living thing that could **drink**. He means that the blood of Pharaoh will soak into the ground. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will make your blood soak into the land where it flows out]

Yahweh says **the channels will be filled from you** as an extreme statement to emphasize how much blood will flow. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and a great amount of your blood will flow into the channels]

The expression **will be filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who will do the action, the first part of the verse indicates that Yahweh will do it. Alternate translation: [and I will fill the channels with your blood]

7.note: Yahweh is speaking as if Pharaoh were a lamp or fire that someone could put out. It means that Pharaoh will die. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at your death]

The word **at** indicates that Yahweh will **cover the heavens** at the same time as Pharaoh’s **extinguishing**, that is, his death. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [at the same time that I extinguish you]

7.q: שֶׁ֚מֶשׁ בֶּ⁠עָנָ֣ן אֲכַסֶּ֔⁠נּוּ וְ⁠יָרֵ֖חַ לֹא יָאִ֥יר אוֹרֽ⁠וֹ
7.note: The implication is that the darkening of the sun, the moon, and the stars is a sign that Yahweh is judging Pharaoh and Egypt. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not make its light shine, as a sign that I am judging you]

8.note: Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **luminaries** that are characterized by **light**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the bright luminaries]

Yahweh is speaking as if **darkness** was something that he could **put** on the land of Pharaoh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will make it dark in your land]
See how you translated **the declaration of the Lord Yahweh** in 5:11.

9.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the **heart** were the place where people think and feel. It means that Yahweh will deeply trouble and anger many peoples. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will make many peoples very upset and angry]

Yahweh is speaking as if Pharaoh were something that Yahweh would break into pieces. This could mean 1) that Yahweh will destroy Pharaoh and cause enemies take him and his people as captives into other nations. Alternate translation: [in my spreading you and your remaining people among the nations] 2) that the news of that destruction will spread among the nations. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in my spreading the news of your destruction among the nations]

10.note: Yahweh is speaking as if **many peoples** were a land that he would make **desolate**. It means that these peoples will be horrified because of what happens to Pharaoh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will cause many peoples to be appalled at you]

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

Yahweh is speaking as if his **sword** could **fly**. It means that Yahweh destroying Pharaoh is like Yahweh swinging his sword in front of these kings to show them that he has the power to destroy them as well. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when I swing my sword in front of them] or [when I threaten them by destroying you]
See how you translated the similar expression in 26:16.

Yahweh is using **a man for his soul** as a common expression of the culture to mean “each one for his own life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each person afraid for his own life]
See how you translated the similar expression in 27:27.

11.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:4.

Here, **sword** represents “the army of the king of Babylon.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The soldiers of the king of Babylon will attack you]

12.note: Here, **fall** represents “die in battle.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will make your multitude die in battle]

The phrase **the ruthless of the nations, all of them** describes the **warriors**, not **your multitude**. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the ruthless of the nations with the information about the warriors. Alternate translation: [all of whom are the ruthless of the nations]

Here, **the pride of Egypt** represents “everything that Egypt was proud of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And they will devastate all the things that Egypt was proud of]

The expression **will be destroyed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who will do the action, the context indicates that the warriors whom Yahweh sends will do it. Alternate translation: [and they will destroy all of her multitude]
See how you translated the similar expression in 28:7.

13.note: Yahweh is using **the foot of man**, one part of a person, to represent people walking through the water. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people walking through the water]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **beast**. He means animals in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the hooves of animals will not stir them up]

14.note: The word **Then** indicates that what Yahweh describes here will happen after he has destroyed the people and animals of Egypt. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [After that]

The point of this comparison is that just as **oil** flows smoothly and slowly, so the rivers of Egypt will flow calmly because no person or animal will stir them up. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and their rivers I will make flow calmly and undisturbed]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:11.

15.q: בְּ⁠תִתִּ⁠י֩ אֶת אֶ֨רֶץ מִצְרַ֜יִם שְׁמָמָ֣ה וּ⁠נְשַׁמָּ֗ה אֶ֚רֶץ מִ⁠מְּלֹאָ֔⁠הּ
15.note: The phrases **a desolation** and **a land desolated from its fullness** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [In my making the land of Egypt completely desolate and empty]
See how you translated this expression in 6:7.
See how you translated the similar expression in 30:12.

16.note: The pronoun **they** refers to **The daughters of the nations**, whom Yahweh mentions in the next sentence. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the daughters of the nations will lament it]

The phrase **The daughters of the nations** refers to those who will sing this funeral song for Egypt. This could mean: (1) the women of the nations, since women in this culture often sang funeral songs. (2) the towns of the nations, since towns are sometimes called the daughters of a nation or city. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The women of the nations will lament it]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:11.

17.note: Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He does not say which month this was. This could mean: (1) the twelfth month, the same month as in the date at the beginning of the chapter. (2) the first month of the year. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [on the fifteenth of that same twelfth month]
See how you translated the similar expression in [32:1](ta:32).

18.q: וְ⁠הוֹרִדֵ֑⁠הוּ א֠וֹתָ⁠הּ וּ⁠בְנ֨וֹת גּוֹיִ֧ם אַדִּרִ֛ם אֶל אֶ֥רֶץ תַּחְתִּיּ֖וֹת
18.note: The implication is that when Ezekiel speaks this message, it will cause Egypt and the other nations to go down to the place where dead people go. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and by speaking this message cause it to go down, it and the daughters of majestic nations, to the lower land where dead people go]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the place where dead people go were a **pit**. It means that Egypt will join those who have died and been buried. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with the ones who have died and been buried]
See how you translated the similar expression in [2:1](ta:02).
See how you translated the similar expression in 26:20.

19.q: מִ⁠מִּ֖י נָעָ֑מְתָּ רְדָ֥⁠ה וְ⁠הָשְׁכְּבָ֖⁠ה אֶת עֲרֵלִֽים
19.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Ask Egypt whom it is more pleasant than, and tell it to go down and be laid down with the uncircumcised]

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that Egypt is no better than any other nation. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You are not more pleasant than anyone else!]

Yahweh is referring to dying and being buried in a polite way by using the phrase **Go down and be laid down**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [Die and be buried with the uncircumcised]

The expression **be laid down** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and lie down among the uncircumcised]

The implication is that being with **the uncircumcised** in death was a disgrace, since it meant lying among people who did not belong to God and who died shameful deaths. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the uncircumcised, who did not belong to God and who died in disgrace]

Yahweh is using the adjective **uncircumcised** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the uncircumcised people]

20.note: Here, **the sword** represents “battle.” The phrase **the slain of the sword** refers to people whom enemies killed in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people killed in battle]

The expression **A sword has been given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who did the action, the context indicates that Yahweh did it. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has given a sword]

The pronoun **her** refers to something that Yahweh does not name. This could mean: (1) Egypt, which enemies will drag away along with all of its people. (2) the **sword**, which enemies will draw out to use against Egypt. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [draw Egypt out and all of Egypt’s multitudes]

21.q: יְדַבְּרוּ ל֞⁠וֹ אֵלֵ֧י גִבּוֹרִ֛ים מִ⁠תּ֥וֹךְ שְׁא֖וֹל
21.note: The implication is that the dead warriors in **Sheol** will speak to Pharaoh to greet him when he arrives there. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The mighty ones of the warriors will greet Pharaoh from the midst of Sheol when he arrives there]
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:20.

22.note: The pronoun **him** refers to Assyria or to its king, even though the previous phrase spoke of Assyria as **her**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [There is Assyria and all of her assembly; all around the king of Assyria are his graves]

23.note: The expression **have been given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who did the action, you could say that people placed their graves there. Alternate translation: [whose graves people have placed in the recesses of the pit]

Yahweh is using **who had given terror in the land of the living** as a common expression of the culture to mean “who terrified people while they were still alive.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who had terrified others while they were alive on the earth]

24.note: Yahweh is using **they bore their humiliation** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they suffered disgrace.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they were put to shame]
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:18.
See how you translated the similar expression in 26:20.

25.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the grave of Elam were a **bed**. It means that people have made a grave for Elam among those who were killed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They have made a grave for her]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because they spread terror in the land of the living]

The expression **He has been put** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who did the action, you could say that people have put Elam there. Alternate translation: [People have put him in the midst of the slain]
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:18.
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:20.
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:24.

26.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 32:25.

27.note: The implication is that these warriors were buried with honor, with their weapons beside them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [who went down to Sheol with honor, buried with the weapons of their war beside them]

Placing the sword of a dead warrior under his head was a symbolic action by which the people who buried him showed that they honored him as a warrior. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And they honored them as warriors by putting their swords under their heads]

Yahweh is using **their iniquities were on their bones** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they remained guilty for their sins even after they died.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they were still guilty of their sins even in death]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe the **terror** that the **warriors** caused in other people, not terror that the warriors felt. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the warriors caused terror]

28.note: The pronoun **you** refers to Pharaoh, whom Yahweh is again addressing directly. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And you, Pharaoh]

The expression **you will be broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who will do the action, the context indicates that Yahweh will do it. Alternate translation: [I will break you]
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:20.
See how you translated the similar expression in 31:18.
See how you translated the similar expression in 31:18.

29.q: אֲשֶׁר נִתְּנ֥וּ בִ⁠גְבוּרָתָ֖⁠ם אֶת חַלְלֵי חָ֑רֶב
29.note: The implication is that even though the kings and leaders of Edom were strong, their strength did not keep them from being killed. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [who have been placed with the slain of the sword, even though they were mighty]

29.q: אֲשֶׁר נִתְּנ֥וּ בִ⁠גְבוּרָתָ֖⁠ם אֶת חַלְלֵי חָ֑רֶב
29.note: The expression **who have been given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who did the action, you could say that people have laid them there. Alternate translation: [whom people have placed, in their might, with the slain of the sword]

Yahweh is repeating the word **They** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [They indeed will lie with the uncircumcised]
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:18.
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:20.

30.q: שָׁ֣מָּ⁠ה נְסִיכֵ֥י צָפ֛וֹן כֻּלָּ֖⁠ם וְ⁠כָל צִֽדֹנִ֑י
30.note: The implication is that **the princes of the north** were the rulers of the nations to the north of Israel. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [There are the rulers of the nations north of Israel, all of them, and every Sidonian]

The implication is that these rulers are now **ashamed**, even though they once used their **might** to terrify people. This could mean: (1) they are ashamed in spite of their might, because their power did not save them. (2) they are ashamed of the terror that their might had caused. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [ashamed even though they once used their might to terrify others]
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:18.
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:20.
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:24.

31.q: אוֹתָ⁠ם֙ יִרְאֶ֣ה פַרְעֹ֔ה וְ⁠נִחַ֖ם עַל כָּל המונ⁠ה
31.note: The implication is that Pharaoh will be comforted when he sees that other nations have also been destroyed, so that his army is not the only one that has died. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Pharaoh will see these other nations that died and be comforted over all of his multitude, because his army is not the only one destroyed]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:11.
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:20.

32.note: The phrase **his terror** is a translation of the way the original text is written. However, the ancient tradition for reading the text aloud has “my terror,” referring to the terror that Yahweh caused. You may want to follow the reading “my terror,” or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [my terror]

The expression **he will be laid down** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language.
